title: Woodward, Shankland Strike; Alice Lee Joins Women's Leaders
summary: GMs Wesley So and Awonder Liang continued as joint leaders with 2.5 points after their mutual encounter ended in a draw in the third round of the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship. GM Andy Woodward was rewarded with a win for his dynamic play against GM Ray Robson, and joined GM Fabiano Caruana in the second-place group with two points. IM Alice Lee benefited from a blunder by IM Nazi Paikidze to score a win and join WGM Thalia Cervantes and FM Megan Paragua at the top with 2.5 points each in the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship. IM Tatev Abrahamyan scored a creditable win against IM Carissa Yip, the defending champion and four-time winner of the tournament, pushing the latter near to the bottom of the table with 0.5 points. None of the players managed to score full points after three rounds in either event, which means that the 'Fischer Prize' of $64,000 awarded to any player winning the U.S. Championship with the same perfect 11/11 score as the legend GM Bobby Fischer from the 1964 national championship is off the table already. The fourth round of each tournament will be on Monday, October 12, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 3: Open Standings After Round 3: Women Round 3 Results: Open We had an interesting reveal from the commentators of the live relay on the favorites to win the tournament. The game between the joint leaders, So and Liang, ended in a draw in 30 moves without much action. In the rest of the games, GM Sam Shankland and Woodward scored impressive victories over GMs Jeffery Xiong and Robson, respectively. Xiong's strategic handling of the middlegame against Shankland was concerning, to say the least. After allowing the creation of an isolated queen's pawn, he also weakened his kingside to accept the traditionally brittle pawn structure with h3-g2-f3. 29...Nxf3! was Shankland's strike to exploit his advantage, which you can find in the notes of GM Dejan Bojkov, who has annotated the Game of the Day.

title: FIDE General Assembly adopts resolution on shorter time controls: What it means
summary: The FIDE General Assembly has formally supported a resolution based on a proposal by the Icelandic Chess Federation concerning shorter time controls in classical chess. However, the adoption of the resolution does not mean that the regulations change immediately. Under the FIDE Charter, the General Assembly is empowered to approve general guidelines for FIDE activities, while amendments to specific rules and regulations fall within the competence of the FIDE Council. The Council will therefore prepare and submit a framework for discussion and approval that implements shorter time controls while allowing for further analysis of their impact. Under the proposed approach, the use of 60 minutes plus 30 seconds per move (60+30) would no longer require special approval. In certain cases, 45+30 would also be permitted. At the same time, two important limitations would remain in place: no more than two games per day for tournaments counting towards titles and norms, and no more than one norm obtained in a tournament played with a shortened classical time control.  Two different sets of requirements  Chess regulations distinguish between two sets of requirements that are often confused. For titles and norms, no more than two games per day are permitted. The reason is straightforward: playing more than two classical games in one day inevitably affects the quality of play, while classical chess, by definition, requires sufficient time for deep thought and considered decisions. For rating purposes only, the restriction is different: no more than 12 hours of play per day. Within this limit, more than two games may be played. This distinction is important. Titles and norms represent some of the most valuable sporting achievements in chess, which is why they are subject to stricter requirements than games submitted for rating alone. In other words, the two-round-per-day limit applies to titles and norms, not to rating as such.  Background Traditionally, the minimum time control for high-level classical tournaments has been 90 minutes for the game plus 30 seconds per move (90+30). In 2026, FIDE introduced a one-year pilot project allowing tournaments, subject to approval by the Qualification Commission, to use 60+30 and, in certain exceptional cases 45+30 while still having the games rated as classical. The pilot responded to practical considerations, including the need to reduce organisational costs and make classical tournaments easier to organise for both players and event organisers. At the same time, an important restriction was introduced: a player may count a maximum of one title norm obtained in a tournament with a shortened classical time control. The remaining norms must be achieved under the regular 90+30 control.  The Icelandic Chess Federation proposal and the General Assembly decision The Icelandic Chess Federation proposed two major changes: making 45+30 a standard classical time control that would not require special approval; allowing three games per day. The Qualification Commission opposed the proposal and recommended that it should not be supported. The FIDE Council instead proposed a compromise: 60+30 would become a guaranteed time control, while 45+30 would remain an exception. Nevertheless, the General Assembly formally supported the Icelandic proposal, with 33 votes in favour, and the resolution is therefore considered adopted. There is, however, an important procedural distinction. The General Assembly sets the general direction, while specific regulatory changes are developed and approved through the FIDE Council. It is also clear that fundamental permanent changes of this kind require broad consensus. FIDE represents more than 200 national federations, and any long-term reform of classical chess regulations should therefore be considered through wide consultation across the chess community.  What the FIDE Council plans to propose The Council’s approach is based on a simple principle: the requirements should reflect the level of the tournament and the quality of play that can reasonably be expected.  60+30 as a general ruleThe Council proposes making 60+30 a guaranteed classical time control, requiring no approval from the Qualification Commission or any other body. Any organiser would be able to use it without requesting special permission.  45+30 for FIDE Circuit tournamentsThe Council proposes automatically permitting 45+30 for tournaments included in the FIDE Circuit and meeting its requirements. These are established, high-level competitions featuring professional players, and the Council considers that a shorter control in such events would not undermine the integrity of classical chess. Organisers would nevertheless be encouraged to take into account the views of players and the specific circumstances of each event.  45+30 for tournaments without players rated 2400 or aboveThe Council also proposes automatically allowing 45+30 in tournaments where no participant has a rating of 2400 or higher. Such events may already use 60+30 under the current framework, so this would represent a moderate adjustment rather than a fundamental change.  No special approval requiredIn the cases above, the shorter time control would apply automatically, without a separate decision by the Qualification Commission.  Two games per day for titles remainFor tournaments counting towards norms and titles, the two-round-per-day limit would remain in place. FIDE considers that it is difficult to maintain the necessary quality of classical chess if players are required to play more than two serious games in one day.  Direct Titles under review The FIDE Council has also asked the Qualification Commission to review the requirements for tournaments awarding Direct Titles. The concern is that norms may become easier to obtain under shorter time controls. A norm achieved at 45+30 is not necessarily equivalent, in sporting terms, to one achieved at 90+30. The Commission will therefore consider whether requirements such as minimum ratings, the number of participants, and the treatment of norms obtained under faster time controls should be adjusted in order to protect the value of international titles.  Openness and next steps The FIDE Council confirms that the General Assembly resolution is being respected and that work on its implementation has already begun. In the near future, the Council intends to approve a formal amendment making 60+30 a guaranteed classical time control. On the remaining issues, the Qualification Commission will be asked to present the arguments both for and against the proposed changes. In line

title: Media accreditation for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship is now open
summary: The Salesforce FIDE World Chess Championship begins on November 22, 2026, in Geneva, Switzerland. The first of 14 games between World Champion Gukesh D of India and Challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will be played on November 24. Two 20-year-old prodigies will battle for the most prestigious title in chess. Media accreditation for the event is now open. To apply, please complete the digital form on the match website. Once submitted, your application will be reviewed by our team. If approved, you will receive a separate confirmation email. Please note that there will be no on-site registration desk at the venue. The online form is the only way to obtain media accreditation. Accreditation will remain open throughout the championship. However, we cannot guarantee timely processing of last-minute applications, so we strongly encourage media representatives to apply in advance. Press accreditation is reserved for professional journalists and media representatives working on behalf of bona fide media organisations. A limited number of accreditations may also be granted to independent writers, bloggers, YouTubers and freelance reporters. If you have previously covered FIDE events, you can expect the usual accreditation procedures and media policies. If this is your first FIDE event, we strongly recommend reading the detailed media guidelines available here. Apply for Media Accreditation: https://worldchampionship.fide.com/media

title: Yu Yangyi beats Ding Liren in final match, wins Shenzhen Masters
summary:
A twelve-player knockout

On 9 October, the Shenzhen Nanshan International Chess Masters 2026 began at the Qiuxian Pavilion in Shenzhen. The tournament was supported by the Chess and Card Games Administrative Centre of China's General Administration of Sport, the Chinese Chess Association, and the Culture, Tourism and Sports Bureaux of Nanshan District and the city of Shenzhen. The competition was organised by the Shenzhen Chess Academy and the Shenzhen Chess Association.

Twelve players competed in a rapid knockout tournament. Each match consisted of four rapid games (15 min. + 10 sec.). If the score was level after four games, a tiebreak with two blitz games (3 min. + 2 sec.) followed. If the score was still level, a deciding game was played with 5 minutes for White and 4 minutes for Black, with a 2-second increment after move 60. A draw was sufficient for Black to be declared the match winner.

Top grandmasters Ding Liren, Yu Yangyi, Wang Hao and Xu Xiangyu were seeded directly into the main tournament. The remaining eight players, all talents born after 2000, competed in a preliminary event. The top four from this stage - Asian champion Kong Xiangrui, Xiao Tong, Huang Renjie and Meng Yihan - qualified for the main tournament.

The other four young players, Peng Xiongjian and Jiang Haochen, as well as the two female players, Zhu Jiner and Yan Tianqi, were eliminated after matches that were in some cases closely contested.

The main stage began on 10 October with the quarterfinals, in which each of the established GMs faced one of the younger talents. The experienced players prevailed in three of the four matches. Kong Xiangrui was the only young player to reach the semifinals.

Ding Liren playing black against Meng Yihan

Former world champion Ding Liren defeated Meng Yihan 3-1. Yu Yangyi beat Huang Renjie 2½-½ after only three games. Wang Hao had more difficulty against Xiao Tong. After a draw and a defeat, the favourite was trailing, but managed to level the match in the third game in a must-win situation. With a victory in game four, Wang Hao also reached the semifinals.

Wang Hao facing Xiao Tong

Yu Yangyi playing white against Huang Renjie

The match between Xu Xiangyu and Kong Xiangrui was the only one to go to extra time. The two players won one game each, while the other two games were drawn. Xu Xiangyu lost the second blitz game and was eliminated.

In the semifinals, Ding Liren defeated Kong Xiangrui 2½-½. Yu Yangyi beat Wang Hao after the first two games of their match had ended in draws, winning both remaining rapid encounters to reach the final.

The final between Ding Liren and Yu Yangyi was a closely contested affair that was only decided in the second tiebreak stage. After four draws in the rapid games, each player won one game in the blitz tiebreak. Yu Yangyi then won the Armageddon game with white.

Wang Hao won the match for third place.

title: Fagernes: Jumabayev takes title, Gloeckler secures second GM norm
summary:
Second GM norm for Gloeckler

Christian Gloeckler (photo below: Anniken Vestby) was one of the leading players in the GM tournament in Fagernes for much of the event. The sixth-seeded German youngster began with three wins, then drew against eventual tournament winner Rinat Jumabayev and continued his strong run with, among other results, a victory over grandmaster Frode Urkedal. After seven rounds, Gloeckler was the sole leader with six points.

In round eight, he held Swedish grandmaster Vitaly Sivuk to a draw. This meant that the 14-year-old had already fulfilled the requirements for his second grandmaster norm. He still had to play the ninth round, however, in order to have played enough games for the norm to count.

Gloeckler then lost with white against Indian grandmaster Krishnan Sasikiran. The defeat cost him the sole lead, but no longer affected the norm: for a GM norm, the result of a nine-round tournament was sufficient.

The tenth and final game did not go as Gloeckler had hoped. He lost again, this time against G. B. Harshavardhan of India. He therefore finished the tournament with 6½ points from 10 games, still a very strong performance.

Harshavardhan v. Gloeckler 1-0

In an equal position, but short of time, Gloeckler went wrong here: 35...Ng6?? cost him the chance of a draw. After 36.f4 Qd8 37.g4 Rc4?+- , the Indian representative converted his advantage confidently and secured third place thanks to scoring 3/3 in the final rounds. Gloeckler was unable to fend off the ensuing attack on his kingside and resigned on move 50 in a hopeless position. With 35...Kh8 followed by ...f5 and ...Nd5, Gloeckler could have kept the highly tactical position balanced.

In the final standings, he finished level with several other players, including Sivuk, Semen Mitusov, Moksh Doshi, Bennet Hagner and Eivind Grunt Kreken. In addition to his second GM norm, Gloeckler also gained 8 Elo rating points.

Gloeckler had already earned his first GM norm in July at the Masters Open in Biel. There he won the tournament with 8/9 points and a performance rating of 2688. With his second norm in Fagernes, he has taken another important step towards the grandmaster title.

At the top of the standings, Rinat Jumabayev, Tiger Hillarp Persson and G. B. Harshavardhan all finished on 7½ points from 10 games. Keyvan Farokhi scored 5½ points and missed the IM norm he had been aiming for. His performance rating of 2389 exactly matched his Elo. Sharan Rao dominates the Open in Fagernes

In the open tournament of the Fagernes International Autumn, top-seeded Indian international master Sharan Rao won convincingly. The clear favourite won his first nine games and had therefore already secured tournament victory before the final round. After defeating Iceland's Hafsteinn Agustsson in round nine, Rao had nine points, two ahead of Ukrainian Stanislav Hohelj, who eventually finished second ahead of Norway's Martin K Andersen. Rao also won his final game and took first place with a remarkable 10/10. A total of 35 players competed in the open section.

The top three in the Open: winner Sharan Rao (centre), runner-up Stanislav Hohelj (left) and Martin K Andersen | Photo: Anniken Vestby

Final standings - Fagernes Open

Tournament information

The Fagernes International Autumn tournament began on 3 October and ran until 11 October at the Scandic Valdres Hotel in Fagernes, around 187 kilometres north of Oslo. The GM section, with 62 players, was played over ten rounds in nine days. The time control was 100 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 40 minutes for the rest of the game, with a 30-second increment from move one. Local player Elham Amar was the top seed with a rating of 2567, followed by Kazakhstan's Rinat Jumabayev (2564) and another Norwegian, Frode Olav Olsen Urkedal (2554). Abhijeet Gupta, G. B. Harshavardhan and Krishnan Sasikiran are the next three players on the starting list, while Aksel Bu Kvaloy and German youngster Christian Gloeckler both have a rating of 2515.

title: US Championships: Shankland and Woodward score
summary:
So and Liang draw, remain as co-leaders

The third round of the US Chess Championship saw the two co-leaders, Wesley So and Awonder Liang, draw their direct encounter, allowing Andy Woodward to join Fabiano Caruana half a point behind them in shared third place. So and Liang remain tied for first place on 2½/3, while Woodward and Caruana stand on 2/3. The round featured two decisive games, as Woodward defeated Ray Robson and Sam Shankland got the better of Jeffery Xiong.

The game between So and Liang was relatively uneventful, with neither player managing to create significant winning chances. Liang, who had the white pieces, had previously defeated Hans Niemann and Sam Sevian, while So had survived difficult positions before beating Sam Shankland and Jeffery Xiong.

Co-leaders Wesley So and Awonder Liang | Photos: Lennart Ootes

The day's most complicated - and entertaining - encounter in the open section was played between Andy Woodward and Ray Robson. Playing black, Woodward adopted an ambitious approach and eventually sacrificed the exchange to obtain active play.

The sacrifice was not entirely sound from an objective standpoint, but it created considerable practical difficulties for Robson, who was already running short of time.

Robson had opportunities to maintain the balance and could have settled for a draw, but continued to look for winning chances. The resulting complications proved difficult to navigate, particularly as the first time control approached. Despite spending considerable time considering his options, Robson first gave up his advantage with h3-h4 and then made the decisive mistake on move 43, as he once again erred by pushing his h-pawn.

Woodward thus secured his first victory of the championship. Having drawn his first two games, Woodward thus moved to 2/3, joining Caruana in the chasing group.

Sam Shankland also collected his first full point of the tournament, defeating Jeffery Xiong with the black pieces. Xiong had begun the event with a victory against Sam Sevian, but subsequently lost to So despite obtaining a promising position. His third-round encounter proved considerably less successful, as Shankland took control in the middlegame and gradually increased the pressure.

Xiong's handling of the pawn structure left him with an isolated central pawn and weaknesses around his king. Shankland exploited these concessions by activating his pieces and creating threats on several fronts.

White's defensive task became increasingly difficult as Shankland's pieces gradually infiltrated his opponent's position. Shankland converted his advantage without allowing meaningful counterplay, bouncing back from his opening-round defeat against So.

Standings after round 3

All games

Women's: Lee joins Cervantes and Paragua in the lead

The women's championship now has three players sharing first place on 2½/3. Alice Lee defeated Nazi Paikidze to catch the previous co-leaders, Thalia Cervantes and Megan Paragua, who both drew their third-round encounters. Anna Zatonskih and Rachael Li follow half a point behind on 2/3.

Lee's victory over Paikidze continued her recovery from a difficult start to the tournament. In round one, she escaped with a draw from a losing position against Yip, while in round two she overcame Jennifer Yu after again finding herself in considerable difficulties. Her third-round encounter featured a one-move blunder which turned Lee's positional edge into a clear material advantage.

Paikidze continued to seek compensation, but her attacking possibilities proved insufficient. With Lee maintaining control and gradually neutralising the remaining threats, Paikidze eventually resigned.

Another significant result came in the encounter between Tatev Abrahamyan and Carissa Yip. Playing white, Abrahamyan obtained a convincing victory over the defending champion, whose difficult start to the competition continued. Yip had missed winning opportunities against Lee in the opening round before losing to 13-year-old Paragua on Saturday. Her third-round game brought another disappointing result.

The encounter featured a sharp middlegame in which Black's ambitious play backfired, as she failed to protect her king in time. In the setup that appeared on the board, White is likely to castle queenside, but given Black's inaccurate middlegame strategy, it was a short castle - played at the exact time - which gave White a clear advantage.

Abrahamyan made effective use of her better-coordinated pieces and central control.

The result was particularly welcome for Abrahamyan, who had lost her opening-round encounter against Cervantes despite obtaining a considerable advantage. Her victory over Yip brought her back to 1½/3, while the defending champion remains near the bottom of the standings with just half a point from three games.

Rachael Li also collected a full point on Sunday, defeating Anna Sargsyan after benefiting from a tactical mistake. Sargsyan had recovered from an opening-round defeat by winning her second game, but failed to maintain the balance against Li.

Li now shares fourth place with Anna Zatonskih on 2/3, half a point behind the three leaders. Cervantes and Paragua, meanwhile, remain unbeaten after following up their two opening victories with draws.
